info.name: Feedrank API
info.description:
A walkthrough of every feature, in order. Each request has a short description and tests, so you can click through and read the responses, or run the whole collection and read the test results.

**Before you start:** run `make up`. If you changed the port or `ADMIN_API_KEY`, update the `baseUrl` and `apiKey` collection variables.

Search responses also show up as a table in the response's **Visualize** tab, with each score broken down.

From a terminal, `make postman` runs the same collection with Newman.

A few things to know:

- The data comes from the live provider endpoints, so tests check rules (ordering, filters, the formula) rather than exact titles.
- The caching requests need Redis, and each needs to run within a minute of the one before it (the cache TTL).
- The rate-limit folder uses up your request budget on purpose and then waits for it to reset, which takes up to a minute. Keep it last.

item.name: 1. Health
item.description: Probes for an orchestrator. Liveness checks nothing but the process; readiness also needs the database. Redis is optional, so neither probe checks it.

request.description: The process is up. It checks no dependencies, so a database outage takes the instance out of rotation instead of restarting it.
The instance can reach Postgres and serve traffic. Answers 503 when it cannot.

item.name: 2. Ingestion
item.description: Ingestion fetches both providers, drops items it cannot trust, scores the rest and upserts them. It runs on start-up and every five minutes; this endpoint triggers a run on demand and needs the admin key.

request.description: A wrong key gets the same answer. The comparison runs in constant time.

Runs ingestion now and reports each provider:

- `fetched`: items that passed validation
- `rejected`: items left out (unknown type, bad date, negative counter); the server logs why
- `changed`: rows actually written

Unchanged rows are skipped, so running this again reports `changed: 0` and leaves the search cache alone. A provider that fails is reported with an `error`; the other one is still stored.

item.name: Two runs at once: one gets 409

exec: pm.test(`Parallel runs answered ${codes.join(' and ')}: one 200, one 409`, () => {

request.description:
Only one ingestion runs at a time, across every instance, thanks to a Redis lock (`SET NX` with a TTL, released by a compare-and-delete script). A run that loses the race gets 409.

Postman sends one request at a time, so after this request the test script starts two more runs side by side and checks that exactly one was refused. Without Redis there is no lock, and both succeed.

item.name: 3. Search
item.description:
`GET /api/v1/search` takes `q`, `type`, `sort`, `page` and `page_size`, all optional. Each result carries its score broken down term by term, so any ranking can be checked by hand.

```
final = base × type_coefficient + engagement + recency
```

exec: pm.test('Without a keyword the sort defaults to popularity', () => {
pm.test('Results are ordered by score, highest first', () => {
pm.test('Pagination defaults to page 1, 20 per page', () => {
pm.test('Each item carries only the counters for its type', () => {

request.description: With no parameters you get every item, highest score first, 20 per page. Each item carries only the counters its type has: views and likes for videos, reading time and reactions for text.

exec: const expected = ({ content_type: type, metrics: m, published_at: publishedAt }) => {
? { base: m.views / 1000 + m.likes / 100, type_coefficient: 1.5, engagement: ratio(m.likes, m.views) * 10 }
: { base: m.reading_time + m.reactions / 50, type_coefficient: 1.0, engagement: ratio(m.reactions, m.reading_time) * 5 };

query.description: the maximum, to check every item

request.description:
The test script recomputes every score from the raw counters and the publish date, and compares each term with `score_breakdown`.

| | Video | Text |
| --- | --- | --- |
| base | views/1000 + likes/100 | reading_time + reactions/50 |
| type coefficient | 1.5 | 1.0 |
| engagement | (likes/views) × 10 | (reactions/reading_time) × 5 |

Recency adds 5 within a week, 3 within 30 days, 1 within 90 days. It is computed when the query runs, so it never goes stale. A zero denominator makes engagement 0.
Filters on the content type.

Provider 2 calls these `article`; ingestion maps them to `text`. Text engagement (reactions per minute of reading) has no upper bound, while video engagement can never exceed 10, so a well-liked article can outrank every video.

item.name: 4. Caching
item.description:
Search pages are cached in Redis for a minute (`CACHE_TTL`). Keys carry a generation number that ingestion bumps whenever it changes rows, which retires every cached page at once. `meta.cached` says whether a response came from the cache.

Run these three in order, each within a minute of the one before. Without Redis, nothing is cached.

exec: // The page size only gives this run a cache key of its own. Taken from
// the clock, it differs between any two runs less than 80 seconds
// apart, which covers the one-minute TTL.
pm.expect(body.meta.cached, 'run the request again in a minute').to.be.false;

request.description: The pre-request script picks an unusual page size, so this request starts with an empty cache entry.

item.description: Errors are RFC 7807 problem documents (`application/problem+json`). Validation reports every problem at once, and each error quotes the request id, which also appears on the server's log lines.

item.name: 7. Rate limiting (run last)
item.description:
Searches are limited per client IP: 120 a minute by default (`RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE`). The counters live in Redis, so every instance shares one budget. If Redis is down, requests are let through rather than refused.

The first request here uses up your budget on purpose; the second waits until it resets. Together they take up to a minute.

exec: const MAX_REQUESTS = 500; // past this, the limiter is clearly off
pm.expect(res.code, 'no 429: is Redis up and RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE above 0?').to.equal(429);

query.description: kept small, since this is sent many times

request.description: After this request, the test script keeps searching until the limiter says no, then checks the 429: a problem document and a `Retry-After` header saying when to come back.

exec: console.log(`Waiting ${seconds}s for the rate-limit window to reset`);

request.description: The pre-request script waits exactly as long as `Retry-After` said, then this search goes through, because the limiter uses fixed one-minute windows.
